english_translation: Things toro zvakavakwa zvakaitwa in / singular dhadhadha that / so that people people wane pekutengera on / at ne things mwe things ri things ne denga it is pasi things noti thing mwe chakapendwa thing mwe.

dialogue.shona: Zvitoro zvakavakwa zvakaitwa mudhadhadha kuti vanhu vawane pekutengera. Pane zvimwe zviri zvine denga riripasi zvinoti chimwe chakapendwa chimwe hachina. Uye chimwe chacho chakaiswa chinhu chinenge tafura pamusoro. Nechepedyo neichocho chinetafura pane zvimusika zviripo zviviri zvisina kurongedzwa zvinhu. Poita chimwe chitoro chihombe chiripo chakavharwa.

grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Past ('zvakavakwa')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'zvakavakwa' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').
grammar_notes.rule: Recent Today Past: [nda- / wa- / ta- / va-] + verb | Earlier Past: [ndaka- / waka- / taka- / vaka-] + verb

grammar_notes.title: Present Tense & Everyday Actions ('zvinoti')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'zvinoti' uses the present marker '-no-'. In Shona, inserting '-no-' between the subject prefix and the verb stem expresses general truths, everyday habits, or states of mind like 'wanting', 'thinking', and 'knowing'. For example: 'ndinoda' ('I want/like'), 'unofunga' ('you think'), 'vanoti' ('they say'), and 'vanorima' ('they farm').
grammar_notes.rule: [ndi- (I) / u- (you) / a- (he/she) / ti- (we) / va- (they)] + -no- + verb -> Ndinoda (I want), Vanogara (They live)

grammar_notes.title: Counting & Numbers in Shona ('chimwe')
grammar_notes.content: In Shona, number words like 'chimwe' always come AFTER the noun they count, and their starting prefix matches the noun's group! The basic number stems are: '-mwe' (1), '-viri' (2), '-tatu' (3), '-na' (4), and '-shanu' (5). For example, when counting people ('vanhu'), you use 'va-': 'munhu mumwe' (1 person), 'vanhu vaviri' (2 people), 'varume vana' (4 men). When counting 'ma-' plurals like 'maminitsi' (minutes) or 'mavara' (colours), you use 'ma-': 'madhongi maviri' (2 donkeys), 'mavara matatu' (3 colours), 'maminitsi mashanu' (5 minutes).
grammar_notes.rule: Noun + Number Stem (-mwe = 1, -viri = 2, -tatu = 3, -na = 4, -shanu = 5) -> vanhu vaviri (2 people), maminitsi mashanu (5 minutes)

active_exercises.prompt: How do you say 'two women and four men' in Shona?
active_exercises.explanation: 'Vakadzi vaviri' = 'two women' (-viri = 2) and 'nevarume vana' = 'and four men' (-na = 4).
